summary: Describes a simple way to make link state routing protocols treat a broadcast network as a point-to-point connection. Choosing the right circuit type matters for adjacency formation, flooding, and how the network appears in the topology. Treating a two-router LAN as point-to-point can simplify things. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5309 explains how to configure a routing protocol to treat a local area network that connects exactly two routers as a direct link between them. That removes the election of a designated router and the extra entry the protocol normally keeps for the shared network.

subtitle: Telling a link state protocol to treat a two-router LAN as if it were a dedicated link.

tldr.problem: Link state protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS treat a LAN as a broadcast circuit, with a designated router and a pseudonode in the topology, even when only two routers sit on it.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes a configuration option that tells the protocol the circuit is point-to-point regardless of the media, and works through what each protocol must then do differently.
tldr.outcome: It removes the designated router election and the pseudonode, and lets the link use unnumbered interfaces, at the cost of the scalability that a shared multi-access network provides.

today: RFC 5309 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It describes an extension that link state protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS use when a LAN connects exactly two routers.

sections.title: Introduction: Two Circuit Types
sections.content:
Point-to-point and broadcast are the two predominant circuit types used by link state routing protocols such as IS-IS and OSPF. The two are treated differently when establishing neighbour adjacencies, flooding link state information, representing the topology, and calculating the Shortest Path First (SPF) and the protocol packets. The important differences are that broadcast circuits use the concept of a designated router and are represented topologically as virtual nodes in the network topology graph.

Compared with broadcast circuits, point-to-point circuits afford more straightforward operation. There is no designated router involved, and there is no pseudonode or network Link State Advertisement (LSA) in the link state database. For IS-IS there is also no periodic database synchronization. Conversely, if there are more than two routers on the LAN media, the traditional view of the broadcast circuit reduces the amount of routing information in the network.

When there are only two routers on the LAN, it makes more sense to treat the connection between them as a point-to-point circuit. This document describes the mechanism that lets link state routing protocols operate using point-to-point connections over a LAN under that condition, and discusses some implications for forwarding IP packets on such a circuit, which it calls a p2p-over-lan circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: A routing protocol has two ways of treating a wire. On a shared LAN it elects one router to represent the segment and adds a placeholder for the segment to its map of the network. On a link with only two routers on it, all of that machinery is unnecessary, and the protocol can be told to act as if the two routers were plugged into each other.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
Although a broadcast circuit is meant to handle more than two devices, there are cases where only two routers are connected over the physical or logical LAN segment: the media itself is being used for point-to-point operation between two routers, which is mainly for long-haul operation; there are only two routers on the physical LAN; or there are only two routers on a virtual LAN. In all of these cases the protocols would normally still treat the media as a broadcast circuit, carrying the overhead of LAN operation without the benefits of reduced routing information and optimised flooding.

Treating a LAN as a point-to-point circuit reduces the amount of information the routing protocol must carry and manage. The election of a designated router or designated intermediate system can be omitted. Flooding can be done as on point-to-point links, without LSA reflection by the designated router in OSPF or the periodic Complete Sequence Number Packets used in IS-IS. Only the connection between the two routers needs to be advertised as a topological entity.

Even when there are multiple routers on the LAN, an operator may want to sub-group them into multiple virtual LANs, which allows different costs to be assigned to the IGP neighbours. When only two routers are in some of those virtual LANs, the IGP can view that LAN as a mesh of point-to-point connections.

The IP unnumbered configuration is widely used in networks. It enables IP processing on a point-to-point interface without an explicit IP address, because the interface can borrow the address of another interface on the node. The advantage is clear in an environment where addresses are scarce, and the unnumbered interface can also be applied over p2p-over-lan circuits. Separating the concept of network type from media type allows LANs such as Ethernet to be unnumbered and so save address space, and it also simplifies network management and configuration. In an IPv6 network, a link-local address used in IS-IS and OSPFv3 serves the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three situations where only two routers share a segment: a link used as a dedicated long-haul circuit, a physical LAN with exactly two routers, and a virtual LAN with exactly two routers. In each case the protocol would otherwise keep a placeholder for the segment and elect a representative. The change also lets the link borrow an address from another interface instead of having its own, which saves addresses and simplifies configuration.

sections.title: IP Addressing on Multi-Access and Point-to-Point Links
sections.content:
When an IP network includes multi-access segments, each segment is usually assigned a separate subnet, and each router connected to it is assigned a distinct IP address within that subnet. The address of a multi-access interface plays three roles. It can be the source IP address, used by the router for locally originated packets destined for that subnet or with a best-path next hop on that subnet. It can be the destination IP address, used by other devices as the destination for packets to router applications such as telnet, SMTP, TFTP, OSPF and BGP. And it acts as a next-hop identifier: when other routers on the same segment forward traffic through that router, their routes carry the interface IP address, which is then used to find the router's MAC address with ARP or Neighbor Discovery. The interface IP addresses help other routers find the data-link details needed to build the frame that carries the packet on the segment.

The IP addressing scheme includes an option that lets administrators assign no subnet at all to point-to-point links, which connect only two devices and use protocols such as PPP, SLIP or HDLC for IP encapsulation. This is possible because routers do not need next-hop identifiers on point-to-point links, since there is only one destination for any transmission, and an interface-independent IP address can serve as both source and destination. Using the unnumbered option for a point-to-point link essentially makes it a purely topological entity, used only to reach other destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: An address on a shared segment does three jobs: it names the router as the source of its own traffic, it gives other devices somewhere to send management and routing packets, and it tells neighbouring routers where to send traffic that passes through this router. On a link with one other router, none of that is needed, so the link can go without an address of its own and simply borrow one.

sections.title: The p2p-over-lan Mechanism
sections.content:
The idea is simple: provide a configuration mechanism that tells the IGP the circuit is of type point-to-point, irrespective of the physical media type. The IGP then sends protocol packets with the appropriate point-to-point information and expects to receive packets as they would be received on a point-to-point circuit. Over LAN media the MAC header must still contain the correct multicast MAC address so that the other side receives it, and in a virtual LAN environment the MAC header must also carry the proper VLAN ID.

For IS-IS, the extension concerns only pure IP routing and forwarding. Because the circuit is physically a broadcast one, the IS-IS packets need MAC addresses, so from the link-layer point of view they remain IS-IS LAN packets. The multi-destination addresses from the IS-IS standard, AllISs, AllL1ISs and AllL2ISs, can be used for link-layer encapsulation, and the use of AllISs is recommended. The circuit needs IP addresses, and the point-to-point IS-IS Hello (IIH) over this circuit MUST include the IP interface addresses. The IPv4 address is the one assigned to the interface for a numbered interface, or the interface-independent address for an unnumbered one; the IPv6 addresses are link-local.

For OSPF and OSPFv3, routers supporting the capability should offer an additional interface configuration parameter specifying the interface topology type. For a LAN interface the interface may then be viewed as a point-to-point interface. Both routers on the LAN simply join the AllSPFRouters multicast group and send all OSPF packets with a destination address of AllSPFRouters, which is 224.0.0.5 for OSPF and FF02::5 for OSPFv3. This is identical to operation over a physical point-to-point link.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is a configuration switch, and each protocol has a little housekeeping to do because the wire is still a LAN. The packets still go out with the LAN's multicast address so that only the other router picks them up, and the protocol's own address information still has to be carried in the hello messages.

sections.title: Compatibility, Detection of Misconfiguration and Deployment
sections.content:
To allow LAN links that connect only two routers to be treated as unnumbered point-to-point interfaces, the MAC address resolution and next-hop IP address issues have to be addressed. Unlike a normal point-to-point IGP circuit, the IP next hop for routes that use the p2p-over-lan circuit as an outbound interface is not optional. It has to be a valid interface or internal address on the adjacent router, and the local router uses it to obtain the MAC address for forwarding. The ARP process must be able to resolve the internal IPv4 address used for unnumbered p2p-over-lan circuits, which means the usual check that the source address of an ARP request sits in the local interface's subnet has to be relaxed for these circuits. In IPv6, Neighbor Discovery resolves the MAC address for the link-local address on the circuit. Where the link state IGP is not configured over the p2p-over-lan link, or the ARP and ND mechanism is not possible, other techniques can be used: a router can be statically configured with the destination MAC address to use on the interface, or the MAC address of the remote device can be gleaned from a data-link frame carrying a packet of the corresponding routing protocol.

Because the difference between a LAN and a point-to-point circuit is now made purely by configuration, early detection of misconfiguration matters. If the circuit is configured as point-to-point and receives LAN hello packets, the router MUST discard them, and if the circuit is a LAN type and receives point-to-point hello packets, it MUST discard those. If the system ID or router ID of an incoming hello packet does not match the one for an established adjacency over a p2p-over-lan circuit, the packet MUST be discarded. If OSPF hello suppression is active for the adjacency, the hello suppression MUST be terminated for a period of RouterIntervalSeconds, after which either the adjacency will time out and an adjacency may be formed with a neighbour with a different router ID, or hello suppression may be renegotiated. Implementations should offer logging and debugging information for these events.

Both routers on the LAN must support the extension and both must have the segment configured as a p2p-over-lan circuit for successful operation. Both SHOULD support at least one of the ways of mapping IP addresses on the link to MAC addresses. If a proprietary resolution method is used by one router, both must be capable of using the same method; otherwise the link should be configured as a standard LAN link with the traditional IGP LAN models.

There are trade-offs when a LAN is modelled as multiple virtual LANs using this extension, since the inherent scalability benefits of multi-access networks are sacrificed. In general it increases the link state database size, the amount of packets flooded, and the route calculation overhead. The technique does bring noticeable benefits for IP address usage, network management and router configuration. Note however that the IP unnumbered option for point-to-point LAN links inherits the same problems as serial links, namely that it is not possible to ping or monitor a specific interface between the routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The two routers must agree, because there is no fallback: if one treats the segment as a LAN and the other as a direct link, the neighbour relationship never forms and the only fix is to change the configuration by hand. The document also says when to expect the change to backfire, since modelling many virtual LANs this way makes the routing protocol carry more state and flood more packets than a shared network would.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no new security issues to IS-IS, OSPF, ARP or Neighbor Discovery. Implementations may have source address subnet checks that need to be relaxed as described in section 4.3. Those checks exist to manage misconfigurations rather than to secure ARP, since an attacker attached to the LAN could pick a subnet-wise correct address as well. If one router on a link thinks the LAN should be either broadcast or p2p-over-lan and the other router has a different opinion, the adjacencies will never form, and there are no fallbacks at either end to resolve the situation except a manual configuration change.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed. The one relaxation the change needs, the source address check in ARP, was never a security control, and an attacker on the segment could satisfy it anyway.
